# Tarav.Diagram

This document describes the current candidate design of `Tarav.Diagram`.
It is subordinate to the Tarav Constitution and remains amendable.

## Data Train

Tarav progressively interprets captured user-agent collaboration through
one integrated data train:

```text
Chat.Raw.Artifact
      ──normalize──▶ Chatlas.Normal.Model
      ──capture─────▶ Diagram.Semantic.Database
      ──select─────▶ Context.Model
      ──supply─────▶ user-agent collaboration
```

Evidence inspection and audit travel in the opposite direction:

```text
Context.Model
      ──expand─────▶ Diagram.Ships / Diagram.Annotations
      ──resolve────▶ Chatlas.Normal.Model
      ──verify─────▶ Chat.Raw.Artifact
```

Meaning accumulates toward the `Context.Model`; evidentiary authority
accumulates toward the `Chat.Raw.Artifact`.

## Progressive Interpretation

`Chat.Raw.Artifact` preserves provider-native evidence. It retains the
greatest source detail while making the fewest Tarav interpretations.

`Chatlas.Normal.Model` turns provider-specific chats into a shared causal
tape of sessions, events, turns, content, and context horizons.

`Diagram.Ships` retain semantic entities and their ordered editions.
`Diagram.Annotations` are a separate collection of typed claims about Ships,
editions, or their relations; an Annotation does not create the subject entity
it describes. An Annotation type may retain an evolving claim lineage of its
own. Ship and Annotation types select the classes that interpret their records
and declare their Assertions.

`Context.Model` selects and organizes relevant Diagram material for a
particular collaboration. It is a contextual projection, not a new
authority surface.

The supplied context enriches further user-agent collaboration, which
captures more touched chat data and continues the loop.

## Responsibility Boundaries

The data train is layered so no component must carry all of Tarav's
complexity:

- `Tarav.Archive` preserves Artifacts without understanding chats.
- Chatlas understands chats without constructing Diagram ontology.
- `Tarav.Diagram` retains typed Ships, assessable claims, and structure without parsing
  provider-native artifacts.
- Contextualization selects useful structure without becoming its
  authority.

Capture therefore precedes interpretation. Higher layers remain
inspectable through lower layers, derived layers can evolve without
rewriting their evidence, and faults in normalization, annotation, or
selection can be surfaced independently.

## Diagram Namespaces

The main `Tarav.Diagram` is composed from `Diagram.Namespace`s. A Namespace is
an independent Git repository containing a flat collection of typed Ships, a
separate collection of Annotations, and the semantic policy used to interpret
both. Namespaces let the same Diagram mechanics serve different semantic
systems without mixing their authority or repository history.

Conceptually:

```text
Tarav.Diagram
  ├── Namespace A repository → Ships + Annotations
  ├── Namespace B repository → Ships + Annotations
  └── Namespace N repository → Ships + Annotations
```

Each Ship and Annotation belongs to exactly one Namespace. A Namespace may
reference records from other Namespaces, but those references do not move or
duplicate the target's authority.

A Namespace owns:

- a stable Namespace identity and human-facing name;
- one independent Git repository and semantic database;
- its accepted Ship and Annotation types and runtime specializations;
- the contracts and Assertions applied to records it contains;
- its support, evidence, addressing, and other semantic policies.

Namespace type allowlists and policies guide normal writers and produce
validation POIs. They do not make the Diagram unwritable: a disallowed,
incomplete, or unassessable record may still be retained while its state is
surfaced as a POI.

Creating a Namespace is analogous to `git init`. It initializes a
self-describing repository with a Namespace definition and empty Ship and
Annotation collections. Mounting that repository into a Diagram load path is a separate,
machine-local operation; creation may perform both operations as a convenience.
Historical storage note (2026-10-19): the former Namespace depot
`~/Documents/tarav/diagram/` was conserved in Archive.Attic Deposit
`16a34bf9-6f2e-4ef2-9536-56955c35b0e7`. Its deposit manifest identifies the
preserved data and obsolete machine-local namespace configuration. The
retired application's repositories remain historical evidence; ordinary
recovery copies material out. This Namespace design is not the current
Lines/Notebook runtime's storage layout.

The Diagram resolves bare Ship or Annotation identities by searching mounted
Namespaces in load-path order. A stable, exact reference includes the
Namespace identity and record identity. Search order is a convenience for
discovery and does not redefine identity.

### Typed Ship Database

A Namespace repository stores all semantic entities in one flat Ship
collection. Models, Blocks, and Lines are Ship types rather than separate
physical tables. Claims about them live in the separate Annotation collection:

```text
<namespace-repository>/
├── .git/
├── namespace.json
├── ships/
│   ├── <ship-uuid>.json
│   └── ...
└── annotations/
    ├── <annotation-uuid>.json
    └── ...
```

Each Ship Record contains its Type, its ordered editions, and only the
structural references required by that Type. Child Ships reference their
parents; parent records need not duplicate child lists. Recursive projection
forms Models, Blocks, Lines, relationships, and later semantic structures from
this flat collection.

Annotations refer to existing Ships, editions, or Annotations. They may
classify a Ship, attach a tag, record review evidence, describe a transition,
or assert another relation. They do not establish the referenced entity's
existence. Annotation types may nevertheless retain their own ordered editions
when the claim itself evolves. This keeps entity history and claims about that
history distinct.

### Line.Annotation

`Line.Annotation` is the first free-standing `Index.Line`. It retains a
natural-language claim like a Block Line, but its context is an explicit
`Argument.Set` rather than one containing Block:

```text
Index.Line
├── Block.Line      → containing Block context
└── Line.Annotation → explicit Argument.Set context
```

Its stable Annotation UUID identifies the claim lineage. Each ordered edition
has its own UUID and retains:

- one nonempty `arguments` array of typed Diagram references;
- `data.text`, the natural-language claim;
- optional producer, `Support.Set`, Gates, Assertions, and score vector.

An Argument reference contains a Namespace UUID, a lowercase `kind` (`ship`,
`edition`, or `annotation`), and the referenced UUID. The generic mechanics
claim only that the arguments contextualize the Line; the natural-language
claim supplies the relationship semantics. More specialized Annotation types
may emerge later without replacing `Line.Annotation`.

The Annotation collection remains physically separate from entity Ships. A
`Line.Annotation` Record uses Ship-like edition mechanics because the claim can
evolve; it still does not create any subject named by its arguments.

The canonical implementation path is a full projection of the authoritative
collections. A later
incremental index may accelerate the same computation, but it must remain
equivalent to the full projector and cannot become a second authority.

### Diagram Object Types

Every retained Ship or Annotation has a `type`; that Type selects the Python
class that owns its structural contract, projection behavior, and Assertions.
Current entity records use Ship types such as:

```json
{"type": "Diagram.Block.Ship", "model_ship": "<uuid>", "editions": []}
{"type": "Diagram.Line.Ship", "model_ship": "<uuid>", "block_ship": "<uuid>", "editions": []}
```

An edition may retain its full Diagram Object.Type name, such as
`Design.Block` or `Design.Line.Principle`. Compact codes remain rendering
conventions only.

Full Type names are record data. Compact codes such as `PR` are rendering
conventions only. Existing records with no Object.Type remain readable through
the generic `Diagram.Block` and `Diagram.Line` classes while surfacing a
missing-Type POI. Unknown, conflicting, or Namespace-disallowed Types likewise
remain writable and recoverable through generic objects while surfacing POIs.

Every Object.Type has two complementary semantic surfaces: an addressable
Definition.Block for Agents and users, and a Python class for executable
mechanics. A class exists only when code must parse or operate on the Type; a
Definition.Block explains intention and meaning. Parametric Record types define
where their Type parameters occur and which values they accept.

The runtime Object.Type registry retains the Definition.Block ship UUID rather
than one Block edition, allowing the definition to evolve through its lineage.
Definition.Blocks resolve through the mounted Diagram, so they need not live in
the consuming project's Model or Namespace. Missing or ambiguous resolution
surfaces a POI without blocking capture.

A Block.Type owns the Line.Type vocabulary valid inside that Block. The normal
design vocabulary belongs to `Design.Block`:

- `Design.Line.Definition` (`DF`)
- `Design.Line.Decision` (`DC`)
- `Design.Line.Constraint` (`CT`)
- `Design.Line.Rejection` (`RJ`)
- `Design.Line.Principle` (`PR`)
- `Design.Line.Freedom` (`FR`)
- `Design.Line.Example` (`EX`)

`Design.Block` does not make its heading a semantic commitment and does not
require a privileged Definition Line. Content gives a Block its semantics;
Type contributes explicit mechanics and assessable conformance claims.

`Diagram.Collection` is a recursive organizational Ship. It may host editions,
reference Diagram objects, and contain other Collections without changing the
semantic home of those objects. Namespace governs, Model models, and
Collection groups.

Edition hosting is independent from semantic attachment. A Line edition may
be hosted by a Collection while its Line Ship remains attached to the Block
that supplies its interpretation context. Model-hosted editions form the
primary Model load; Collection-hosted editions are discovered through
Collection expansion or explicit queries.

`Impl.Req.Collection` is the bounded organizational surface for one
implementation request. It hosts supported User-Touched editions accumulated
across design and execution while allowing those Lines to remain attached to
suitable existing Model Blocks. A numerical label such as `502.Impl.Req` is a
human-facing address; the Collection ship UUID remains its identity.

The Block is not the implementation's main coordination artifact. The Agent
maintains a separate live-note `Impl.Req` containing `Impl.Abstract`, an
`Impl.Req.Diagram` reference to the Collection and Draft, `Execution.Plan`, and `Impl.Log`.
Agent-only plans, status, logs, summaries, and incidental observations may live
there without becoming User-Touched Diagram Lines. During design and execution,
the workflow reconciles only relevant material grounded in the corresponding
User-Touched chat data.

An Impl.Req Collection has `Open` or `Closed` lifecycle state. Open work may be
reconciled freely in its Draft. Closing makes it a bounded historical edition;
normal later writes and reopening outside its declared window surface POIs.
They do not make the Diagram mechanically unwritable. The older
`Impl.Req.Block` remains readable for compatibility but is not the target for
new implementation capture.

`Issue.Block` is the addressable Diagram surface for a temporary concern such
as an idea, reminder, question, opportunity, defect, migration, or
contradiction. Parking is a workflow that creates an `Issue.Block`; it does not
introduce a `Parking.Note` Object.Type or separate storage surface.

Initially, `Issue.Block` accepts the Design-family Line.Type vocabulary and the
specialized `Issue.Line.Resolve` Type. An Issue projects as open until a Resolve
Line has a passing reviewed `Verbatim.Gate`. A missing, failed, or unassessable
review leaves the Issue open and surfaces an `issue-open` POI without blocking
mutation. A later ordinary Line does not stale a passing resolution.

Each Ship or Annotation class owns how its record contributes to a projected object.
Projected Line and Block assertion surfaces recursively expose the Assertions
of their contributing Annotations and contained objects. Assertion identities
are preserved so a linter can evaluate by level without evaluating one
Assertion twice.

### User-Touched Chatlas Index

`User.Touched.Chatlas.Index` is the first, default, and fundamental Namespace.
It uses Chatlas as its evidence model and projects the Model/Block/Line
knowledge structure grounded in `User.Touched.Data`.

Other Namespaces may use unrelated semantics, Annotation types, and support
policies while reusing Diagram identity, storage, specialization, assertion,
scoring, querying, and POI mechanics. This allows speculative or Agent-authored
material to remain available without polluting the User-Touched index.

## Chatlas Foundation

Chatlas is an integral part of Tarav and the native evidence model of the
`User.Touched.Chatlas.Index` Namespace.

Chatlas captures selected provider-native material into a Git-tracked raw
repository suitable for registration by `Tarav.Archive`. It then derives
the normalized causal tape used by the Diagram.

Supported Ship editions and Annotations in this Namespace use Chatlas
references for support and producer coordinates rather than direct references
into provider-native Artifacts. A Chatlas reference
must remain able to resolve its normalized subject and expose the Archive
references supporting it.

Conceptually:

```text
Diagram supported record
      ↓ Support.Set / Producer
Chatlas.Reference
      ↓ normalized subject and provenance
Chatlas.Normal.Model
      ↓ source evidence
Archive.Reference
      ↓
Chat.Raw.Artifact
```

For every member of a record's `Support.Set`, the referenced content
must have been present in the record's producing chat context before
the producing turn. This is assessed by resolving the support content and
inspecting the producer's preceding chat horizon; it does not require a
separate materialization record.

### Rooted Support Sets

In `User.Touched.Chatlas.Index`, a supported record's `Support.Set` is a set of
rooted support members. Every member designates one `User.Turn` as its root and
may select a bounded neighborhood of companion User or Agent turns needed to
interpret that touch.

```text
Support.Set
└── Support.Member
    ├── root: User.Turn
    └── neighborhood: selected companion User or Agent turns
```

The root establishes the qualifying `User.Touch`. Neighborhood turns preserve
interpretive context but do not replace that root. When several User turns
independently support a record, they may be represented by several rooted
members rather than one unstructured collection of messages.

Support references must identify both the Chatlas session and exact Turn
edition they address. This permits the Diagram to resolve cross-chat support,
render each selected neighborhood in causal order, and let consumers expand
beyond that selection when necessary.

A later User touch does not retroactively enter an older edition's producing
context. It is recorded through a new edition on the same Ship or through a
new Annotation about the existing Ship, depending on whether the entity itself
changed.

## Monolithic Library

Tarav is one monolithic library. Archive, Chatlas, Diagram, and
Contextualization are responsibility and data boundaries rather than
separate packages or services.

Diagram Ships and Annotations are retained as typed data and instantiated by
the Tarav library as runtime objects. The retained data stores irreducible
instance-specific facts. Namespace- and type-level rules and reliably
recoverable values may be supplied or derived by code. Data is duplicated only
when a material robustness benefit justifies it.

The only universally required retained field inside either collection is
`type`:

```json
{
  "type": "<Ship.Type or Annotation.Type>"
}
```

This is the minimum common field, not a prohibition against additional fields.
Ship editions, producer, support, location, payload shape, and other facts
belong to the containing Namespace or specialized Type. A record's identity
comes from its address, and its Namespace comes from the repository containing
it; neither needs to be duplicated inside retained data.

The constitutional requirement that Diagram semantic material link to archived data
does not require one universal retained field. A Namespace may retain or
reliably derive that linkage according to its own model. Missing or
unresolvable archival grounding must surface through its Assertions and POIs;
it does not prevent the writable Diagram from retaining the Annotation.

Generic Ship and Annotation runtime objects expose only identity, Namespace,
declared Type, and opaque retained Record. Their Namespace supplies base
Assertions and specialization behavior. Specialized Types may add Assertions
but cannot remove Namespace requirements.

Support is not a universal Diagram field or status. A Namespace may define
direct User support, support derived through referenced Diagram objects,
mechanical support, or another policy. Support status remains distinct from
Assertion scoring: `UnAsserted` means that required Assertion scores are
missing or unresolvable, not merely that direct User support is absent.

### Runtime Type Specialization

One retained Ship Record is loaded first as a generic `DiagramShip`; one
Annotation Record is loaded as a generic `DiagramAnnotation`. Generic loading
does not require the runtime to understand the declared Type.

When a consumer needs type-specific behavior, it explicitly specializes that
object:

```python
ship = diagram.ship(ship_id)
typed_ship = ship.specialize()

annotation = diagram.annotation(annotation_id)
typed_annotation = annotation.specialize()
```

`specialize()` asks the record's Namespace to select a registered class from
the retained `type`. The specialized class is the code-owned home for that
Type's parsing, navigation, Assertions, and other behavior.

Specialization is strict. An unknown type or data that does not satisfy its
registered class raises an ordinary error. Generic access remains available,
but Tarav does not prescribe whether the caller should retain it, report the
error, skip the Record, or stop its operation.

## Gates and Review

A Gate is a reusable set of mechanically evaluated Assertions over retained
collaboration evidence. Gate evaluation never blocks Diagram mutation. Failed,
missing, and unassessable Gate Assertions surface POIs.

`Verbatim.Gate` is a proxy for explicit User review of one exact Line wording.
Its retained instance data is:

```json
{
  "type": "Verbatim.Gate",
  "token": "<opaque-token>",
  "proposal_turn": "<Agent Chatlas.Turn.Reference>",
  "approval_turn": "<User Chatlas.Turn.Reference>"
}
```

The token is an opaque nonce, not a content hash. The Gate passes only when
the proposal resolves to an Agent turn containing both the token and
materially equivalent Line wording, and a later User turn in the same chat
explicitly approves that token.

A newly captured `Diagram.Line.Ship` edition may retain its Gates directly.
Reviewing an immutable existing Line edition creates a separate claim:

```json
{
  "type": "Diagram.Line.Gate.Annotation",
  "target_edition": "<existing Diagram.Line.Ship edition UUID>",
  "gates": [{"type": "Verbatim.Gate", "...": "..."}]
}
```

The target edition supplies the wording, Model, Block, and Line lineage. The
gate Annotation does not create, rebind, or duplicate that target. One review exchange may
cover several Lines; each exact target receives its own independently
assessable gate-only Annotation.

Gate records retain no authoritative passed flag. Tarav recomputes Gate
standing from the target record and Chatlas evidence. A Line ship is
`Reviewed` when at least one exact Line edition in that lineage has a
passing `Verbatim.Gate`. Later ungated lineage members do not erase that
standing; their continuity remains a separate Assertion.

`Capture.Authorization.Gate` records that a User authorized one workflow to
perform a bounded class of Diagram writes. It retains the permission Turn, the
literal invocation token, workflow, operations, and target scope. Affected
editions reference its UUID, and the Capture.Receipt publishes that coverage.
Its evaluator checks User role, token presence, and scope resolution.

Authorization is orthogonal to wording review, semantic support, and Assertion
quality. An explicit `--impl --exec` may authorize automatic capture without
approving any exact Line wording.

Capture has no Gate-specific command path. A `Capture.Manifest` transports
typed Ship updates and Annotation records without interpreting their
semantics. The Namespace specializes each record from its `type`; the
resulting Tarav class owns its
schema, model location, Assertions, mechanical checks, and POIs. Gate
Annotations therefore travel through the ordinary Capture path without adding
Gate commands or Gate branches to Capture.

## Assertion Evaluation

`Assertion.Engine` is the central read service for current Assertion state.
Ship and Annotation types declare Assertions, registered evaluators implement
their mechanical assessment, and the Engine resolves available evidence and
produces current score vectors.

Renderers, linters, contextualizers, and other consumers request Assertion
state from the Engine. They do not evaluate Gates or other Assertion types
independently.

The Engine combines retained scores with mechanically recomputed scores without
writing derived truth into the authoritative Ship or Annotation Record. A mechanically
derived result may be cached as disposable data, but it is never authoritative
Annotation content.

Assertion state distinguishes `NotEvaluated`, when no score or applicable
evaluation result exists; `Unassessable`, when evaluation lacks resolvable
evidence; `Passed` and `Failed` Boolean scores; and other `Scored` values.

A semantic record remains `UnAsserted` while any required Assertion is
`NotEvaluated` or `Unassessable`. A falsy score is still an asserted result and
surfaces a POI without making Diagram mutation invalid.

## Named Renderers

Diagram Renderers are named, read-only code projections over Diagram objects.
They create no Annotations and hold no Diagram authority. Several Renderers may
present the same object differently without requiring their surfaces to agree.

Each Renderer declares a stable name, accepted target kind, output media type,
and implementation. Renderer selection is explicit:

```bash
tarav diagram render \
  --line-ship <uuid> \
  --renderer Kernel.Writing.Line.WithSupport
```

Renderer discovery is mechanical through `diagram renderer list` and
`diagram renderer show`. Native output is written to stdout; `--json` returns
an envelope containing the Renderer name, target, media type, content, and
POIs.

A Line Renderer projects the current Line state from the latest ordered
edition in its Ship Record. It does not erase the lineage: `diagram ship show`
exposes every retained edition when history is relevant to Agent reasoning.
Alternative historical or comparative Renderers may present several editions
explicitly, but ordinary HEAD rendering follows the current projection.

Support-aware Renderers preserve exact rooted Chatlas verbatims and navigation
references. Contextualizing Renderers include available Assertion scores and
surface `UnAsserted` state rather than hiding it.

## Context Views

`Diagram.View` is a retained contextual projection over Diagram Ships. It is a
separate Git-backed WIP surface: it selects and materializes context for an
Agent without becoming a Ship or Annotation in the semantic database, or an
authority over that database.

The current View repository schema is v2:

```text
<views-repository>/
├── repository.json
└── <view-ship-uuid>/
    ├── manifest.json
    ├── about.json
    ├── config.json
    └── view.json
```

`manifest.json` is a `Diagram.View.Manifest`; its `id` identifies the
descriptor while `view_ship` identifies the retained View. Materialized Line
history in `view.json` refers to semantic-database editions with
`edition_id`, never `annotation_id`. `source_editions` records the exact
Namespace commits from which the View was materialized.

Schema migrations advance the complete retained View repository. Normal View
mechanics consume only the current schema; the one-boundary migration code is
kept separate from runtime loading and projection.

## User-Touched Semantic Lineages

`User.Touched.Chatlas.Index` is intended to support a knowledge graph grounded
in `User.Touched.Data`. A chronological chat tape alone is not sufficiently
structured for contextualization, while a current graph without its reasoning
history loses how the user's ideas developed.

The current semantic hierarchy is a recursive collection of typed Ships:

```text
Model
  └── Block
        └── Line

Annotations
  └── claims about a Ship, edition, transition, or relation
```

`Diagram.Model.Ship`, `Diagram.Block.Ship`, and `Diagram.Line.Ship` are stored
in the same flat collection. A Block Ship refers to its Model; a Line Ship
refers to its Model and Block. Recursive projection discovers children through
those references. An addressable Line contains its ordered statement editions;
a Block groups Lines into a larger semantic unit; a Model groups Blocks into a
consumable interpretation for a project, question, or other purpose.

Each Ship identity establishes one semantic lineage. Each edition has its own
UUID within that Ship. The current record can therefore retain a rename or
other evolution without changing the entity's address and without asking an
Annotation to create the entity.

Annotations are independent claims about existing Ships or editions. Their
identity addresses the claim, not the subject. A rename Annotation may relate
two Model editions; a tag Annotation may classify a Ship; a Gate Annotation
may add review evidence to one exact Line edition. The Ship history remains
intelligible even when richer relationship vocabulary is deferred to Agents.

Object.Types may be assigned after content capture through support-free
curation Annotations:

```json
{
  "type": "Diagram.Block.Type.Annotation",
  "location": {"model_ship": "<uuid>", "block_ship": "<uuid>"},
  "block_type": "Design.Block"
}
```

```json
{
  "type": "Diagram.Line.Type.Annotation",
  "location": {
    "model_ship": "<uuid>",
    "block_ship": "<uuid>",
    "line_ship": "<uuid>"
  },
  "line_type": "Design.Line.Constraint"
}
```

These Annotations add no entity or wording and require neither a `Support.Set`
nor a producer chat. They reference existing Ships whose content retains
its own support, contribute only to Object.Type projection, and expose a
Type-conformance Assertion. Missing or poor conformance scores surface POIs
without blocking the assignment.

Model and Block Ship creation is structural bookkeeping and need not carry a
producer or direct `Support.Set`. Their projected support comes from supported
Line editions and applicable Annotations. A later semantic operation on a
Ship may add an edition, an Annotation, or both: the edition records what the
entity becomes; the Annotation records a claim about the transition.

`Line`, `Block`, and `Model` identities are semantic lineages rather than
fixed wordings or fixed collections. Their identities persist through
editions. An edition may rephrase an idea, add or remove material, or reflect
the evolution of the user's position without requiring a new identity.

This is the Ship-of-Theseus problem applied at every grouping level. The
fundamental lineage claim is:

> Despite these changes, treating these editions as the continuing history
> of one addressable thing remains semantically coherent.

Continuity is not semantic equivalence. Two expressions may differ or even
record a changed user position while remaining useful parts of one semantic
history. Conversely, superficially similar material may require separate
lineages when grouping it as one continuing thing would be incoherent.

The system must preserve these continuity claims as assessable Assertions.
The expected assertion is strongest and most local at the Line layer and may
become broader as Lines are grouped into Blocks and Blocks into Models.

### Project Model

A Tarav project may name one default Model ship in `.tarav/project.json`:

```json
{
  "diagram": {
    "main_model": "<model-ship-uuid>"
  }
}
```

The project configuration retains only the Model ship UUID. It is an
association, not an ownership claim: several Projects may point to the same
main Model. For example, implementation and documentation Projects belonging
to one system may share one system Model while retaining independent Project
identities and repositories.

The Model Ship determines the Namespace that owns the Model, so
Capture does not need a second Namespace target. Associating a Project with an
existing Model does not create, copy, or modify that Model.

If `main_model` is missing, the Project may be associated with an existing
Model or a Capture bootstrap may allocate a Model Ship in the default
`User.Touched.Chatlas.Index` Namespace and retain
the UUID in the project configuration. Model creation and Project association
remain distinct operations even when one command performs both as a
convenience. A Model with no Line material is an existing empty Model, not a
reason to allocate another identity. A configured Model that cannot be
resolved must surface an error or POI and must not be silently rebound.

Model and Block Ship records may lack direct `User.Touch` support. Their
Namespace still supplies assessable base Assertions, and their
projected support is derived from the User-supported material attached within
them. This structural exception does not permit ordinary semantic Line
Line editions to bypass the Namespace's direct-support policy.

## Bad Indexing and Semantic Evolution

Legitimate semantic evolution and incorrect annotation are different
conditions.

Within `User.Touched.Chatlas.Index`, a supported edition or Annotation that does not honestly
follow from its producing context and declared support is `Bad.Indexing`. It
should be surfaced as a POI and may be amended, replaced, marked, or pruned.
Git history may preserve the former data, but the Namespace must not present an
unsupported record as a valid edition of the user's evolving idea.

A correctly grounded earlier position followed by a correctly grounded
later position is legitimate semantic evolution. The earlier edition may
remain in the lineage even when the later position differs from it.

For every member of a record's `Support.Set`, the referenced content
must have been available in the producing Agent's chat context before the
producer turn. Cross-chat support is valid only when the referenced content
was brought into that producing context. This makes it possible to audit
that an Agent derived an Annotation from material it actually received
rather than merely copying support references.

## Context-Local Capture

The current Capture design concerns `User.Touched.Chatlas.Index` and only the
Model or Models being worked on in the producing chat context. It does not
predict how unengaged or future Models may reuse the captured material.

The `NOW` of one capture is the complete bounded context available to the
annotating Agent at its producer turn. A NOW may contain earlier chats,
Models, files, tool results, and other addressed material loaded into the
current chat. The record's `Support.Set` selects the high-signal
`User.Turn`s supporting its claim from within that context.

Every semantic Line edition or Annotation produced by Capture is therefore an
interpretation made in one auditable NOW. The Namespace accumulates Ship
history and claims from successive NOWs rather than constructing one timeless
interpretation of the user.

Capture performs only the minimum ontology work needed to locate the
record in the context being developed. A captured Line edition is
assigned to a Line ship, a Block ship that contextualizes it, and a Model in
the active capture scope. Capture may work on several Models in one session,
but it concerns only those explicitly engaged Models.

Cross-model reuse, derivation, dependency, mixture, and forking are not
prospective Capture responsibilities. When a later user-agent collaboration
uses one Model to construct or interpret another, that relationship belongs
to the future NOW. It may then be represented through ordinary grounded
Ships and Annotations, including relationship Blocks whose Lines reference related
Diagram objects.

Tarav must provide stable references and navigation primitives that let
Agents describe such relationships. It need not hard-code their semantic
vocabulary into Capture.

## Diagram Draft and Capture Manifest

`Diagram.Draft` is a durable, mutable, and checkable writing workspace over one
Model. It owns candidate Ship and Annotation changes. Checking projects the
Draft as an overlay without mutating the Diagram; applying it compiles an
internal `Capture.Manifest`, writes once, and retains the `Capture.Receipt`.

Materialize a Draft when a persistent writable semantic workspace becomes
useful, not merely because capture discussion began:

- reviewed capture creates a short-lived Draft after `::land`;
- automatic capture may create and immediately apply a short-lived Draft;
- implementation capture maintains one durable Draft across slices and applies
  it once at completion.

User-Touched reviewed Capture remains an approval-gated collaboration performed
in chat. The User and Agent discuss, revise, and approve each Block and Line
there before a Draft is materialized.

A `Capture.Manifest` does not exist during that semantic discussion. After the
User sends `::land`, the Agent materializes a Draft; its apply operation
compiles the Manifest as an internal faithful transport format. The Manifest is
neither a collaboration surface nor a Diagram authority surface.

Conceptually:

```text
User/Agent discussion in chat
          ↕ propose / group / revise / approve
Settled capture proposal
          ↓ explicit ::land
Agent materializes Diagram.Draft
          ↓
Overlay check + internal Capture.Manifest compilation
          ↓
Capture applies Ship editions and Annotations
          ↓
semantic claims initially remain UnAsserted
          ↓ later
Semantic Assertion scoring
          ↓
Scores + POIs + curation
```

Before landing, Tarav tooling should provide read-only Model projections and
manifest-ready context fragments: Chatlas references, resolved hashes, Diagram
identities, and existing Model, Block, and Line objects. After `::land`, it
should provide an empty Manifest template and freshly minted UUIDs. The Agent
should not reconstruct mechanical bureaucracy by hand.

The Draft and compiled Manifest identify their target Model ship. Resolving that Model identifies
the Namespace repository that owns it and therefore the sole write destination
for the batch. The Manifest does not need a redundant Namespace target.

The Manifest has two record collections:

```json
{
  "class": "Tarav.Diagram.Capture.Manifest",
  "schema_version": 2,
  "model_ship": "<uuid>",
  "ships": [
    {
      "id": "<line-ship-uuid>",
      "type": "Diagram.Line.Ship",
      "model_ship": "<model-ship-uuid>",
      "block_ship": "<block-ship-uuid>",
      "editions": [{"id": "<edition-uuid>", "data": {"text": "..."}}]
    }
  ],
  "annotations": []
}
```

`ships` creates new semantic entities or appends editions to existing ones.
`annotations` adds claims about existing Ships or editions. Reusing a Ship UUID
claims semantic continuity; every new edition receives a fresh UUID.

Semantic capture remains Agentic work, but it occurs in the approved chat
discussion. Post-land Manifest construction may choose mechanical identities
and serialize the result, but it must not introduce new semantic content. If a
mechanical correction requires semantic reinterpretation, landing stops and
the work returns to discussion and approval.

The compact Agent landing-pause turn before `::land` serves as the producer
coordinate for its supported records. It need not repeat the approved proposal:
its context must already contain the exact approved proposal turns and
supporting User turns. `::land` authorizes materialization; it does not
retroactively supply semantic support or approval.

Manifest checking covers `Mechanical.Semantics`: schema shape, resolvable
references, hashes, reference sides, producer-context inclusion, target
existence, batch-local references, unique identities, and executable
ordering. It may help the Agent revise the Manifest, but it cannot certify
semantic quality.

> Mechanical code may verify that a semantic act is well-formed, traceable,
> and executable; it cannot certify that the semantic act is good.

Applying a Manifest revalidates its mechanical interpretation and
materializes the mechanically executable batch. Formal semantic assessment
is always later work performed through the Semantic Assertion system. Newly
captured records ordinarily remain `UnAsserted` until their Assertions receive
a score vector; that ordinary state may surface POIs
but does not make capture a semantic-scoring workflow.

Git commit policy is an apply-time option, not Manifest data. Normal Capture
application writes and commits the batch in its Namespace repository. A
development caller may explicitly request an uncommitted application; this
changes only materialization behavior and leaves the Manifest unchanged.
Uncommitted records are outside a stable Diagram version until the
developer commits them through Git.

## Models and HEADs

There is no single mechanically derived `Tarav.Diagram.HEAD`.

Different projects, questions, and consumers may construct different Models
from the same normalized tape and Diagram material. These Models may make
different compatible or incompatible selections while remaining grounded in
the same evidence.

The ordinary working projection uses the last ordered edition of each Ship as
its current edition. `ship show` and audit mechanics expose the full ordered
history. A contextual View may select or retain another presentation without
becoming the authority for the Ship. Branching history remains a later
extension rather than hidden selection logic in the linear v2 Record.

Capture updates only the Models in its active scope. Model composition and
cross-model relationships are interpreted when a user-agent collaboration
works on them; Capture does not maintain or propagate speculative future
dependencies.

## Open Design Boundaries

The following mechanics remain deliberately unresolved:

- how an Annotation identifies the exact Block edition that contextualized
  its wording;
- whether and how one Annotation or Line may participate in several Blocks;
- how forks and later reunification of semantic lineages are represented;
- how continuity Assertions are evaluated and scored at each layer;
- how Agents construct, update, and compare Model HEADs;
- the exact primitives through which future NOWs express Model composition
  and cross-model relationships without expanding Capture's responsibility.

These are implementation and further-design questions. They must preserve
the grounded reasoning tape, plural agent-constructed Models, assessable
continuity, and the distinction between semantic evolution and Bad Indexing.

## Preamble

This document is the Constitution of Tarav.

It states the fundamental principles and boundaries of the Tarav system. Any surface claiming to be part of Tarav must comply with this Constitution.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb c3bd772ca1ca -->

The Constitution is intentionally general, incomplete, and amendable. It does not contain all Tarav design truth or require a single implementation.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb ecd16660e190 -->

When a Tarav design conflicts with the Constitution, the conflict must be surfaced. It can be resolved by changing the design, amending the Constitution, or changing both.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 1c3656d59617 -->

## Purpose

Tarav is an external `Agents.Harness` intended to enhance collaboration between Users and Agents. It provides tools and workflows addressing recurring problems in that collaboration.

Concretely, Tarav is an extensible Python library. Its capabilities can be integrated into a wider system and composed into specialized harnesses for particular Projects.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 529226730418 -->

Capture, including recording `User.Touched.Data`, annotation primitives, contextualization, checks, and workflow coordination are concrete capabilities through which Tarav supports collaboration. They can evolve while remaining consistent with this purpose.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 3d347443ec3e -->
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb f8a6d1c8c52c -->


## Projects

A `Project` is a fundamental Tarav concept. Tarav's capabilities can be selected, extended, and combined to build a harness for a particular Project.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 8178981fa771 -->

## Agent Harness Boundary

An Agent is a harness around an LLM. Tarav is an `Agents.Harness`: a harness around Agents that supports collaboration between those Agents and Users.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb e1afd7dc0934 -->

Tarav may provide mechanisms for launching or operating Agents, but agent execution is not its defining responsibility.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 7353b15ca16e -->

Tarav supports the contextualization of agent reasoning; it does not prescribe the internal reasoning of an Agent.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb e0644e75d73d -->

## Mechanical and Agentic Work

Tarav must use deliberately simple, bounded code to perform work that can be specified reliably and to provide data, context, and signals to flexible Agents.

Tarav should mechanize as much of the common case as practical without encoding complex or brittle solutions merely to avoid Agent involvement.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 193b02b6c8d2 -->

Ambiguous, interpretive, open-ended, and long-tail work should be routed to Agents.

Agent fallback is an intended part of Tarav architecture, not a failure of mechanical automation.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 49fa142669d1 -->

## User Context

Tarav is biased toward enriching agent context with `User.Touched.Data`. It must help agents work as fully contextualized on the user as possible.

This grounding does not claim that `User.Touched.Data` is authoritative or correct. Tarav does not prescribe how an agent reasons from that context.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb e638ee17754d -->

## Natural Workflows and Extensibility

Tarav must fit `User.Natural.Workflows` rather than require users to adopt one prescribed Tarav workflow.

Tarav must be flexible and designed for extension so users, agents, and implementations can adapt it to their natural collaboration patterns.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb c0c3c12db0f2 -->

Extensions may introduce different mechanisms and workflows, but any surface claiming to be part of Tarav remains bound by this Constitution.

## Session Goals

Tarav-supported user-agent sessions may pursue both the user’s immediate objective and the capture and enrichment of `User.Touched.Data`.

The user controls the foreground workflow. Tarav must not stop or redirect product development to require Diagram enrichment.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 177f4e2677c5 -->

When the user chooses development, the session develops. Enrichment may occur organically without obstructing that work. When the user chooses capture, curation, or enrichment, the session pursues that work directly.

Tarav must provide primitives that make collecting, annotating, and curating `User.Touched.Data` cheap and organic within `User.Natural.Workflows`.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb bfab21d025fb -->

Completeness measures may guide enrichment and surface opportunities, but they must not gate work or impose a globally complete Diagram.

## Mutation and Validation

Tarav must be evolvable and migration-friendly. Its code, schemas, and data are amendable. For product surfaces, committed Git history together with retained work conversations is sufficient change evidence by default. Additional documentation or tracking may be added when useful, but exhaustive change explanations must not become a prerequisite for evolution.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 823eddb6a42f -->
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb a1e213b405af -->

The nonblocking validation commitment for capturing user data is stated in Capture First below.

Users, agents, and other consumers are the primary mutators of Tarav state.

## Checks and Findings

Tarav must provide extensible checking capabilities that help users and agents assess a Project’s state and surface findings with enough context to act on them.

Specific workflows define what gets checked, when checks run, and how findings are represented. A finding does not itself dictate the response; users, agents, and other consumers decide how to interpret and act on it.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 69c072923d44 -->

## Capture First

Tarav prioritizes recording `User.Touched.Data`. When data may contain or preserve `User.Touched.Data`, capture must occur before concerns about completeness, formatting, annotation quality, or other POIs are resolved.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 88630183a7af -->

Tarav capture must favor recoverable overcapture over irrecoverable failure to record touched data.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 627d3007ee2b -->

Validation must not block the capture of user data. Tarav considers this data highly valuable. When a capture path fails, the system must provide a simpler fallback, including retaining raw data for later processing. Capture comes first; validation and organization can follow.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 45e1f418f101 -->
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 96e54d858b65 -->

Once data enters Tarav, it may be curated, annotated, amended, enriched, and scored over time.

Tarav is not a general repository for Agent-generated summaries or content. Agent-generated data is not archived merely because it was generated; it may be archived when touched, deliberately selected, or captured as a safety margin against losing touched data.

## Logistical Extensions

Tarav must support integration with databases, query systems, and other logistical extensions that improve performance and access over Tarav data.

Tarav data remains authoritative. Logistical extensions may index, cache, query, or project that data, but they do not displace its authority.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 287596d1a3ec -->

## Collaboration Loop

Tarav is organized around a continuous collaboration loop:

```text
user-agent collaboration
          ↓ captures
       Touched.Data
          ↓ recorded by
      Tarav.Archive
          ↓ structured by
      Tarav.Diagram
          ↓ selected through
     Contextualization
          ↓ enriches
  user-agent collaboration
```

## Tarav.Archive

The main responsibility of `Tarav.Archive` is to record `User.Touched.Data`.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb a8662815421f -->

`Tarav.Archive` registers `Archive.Artifact`s and retains `Archive.Record`s about them.

An `Archive.Artifact` is the actual data identified by the Archive. An Artifact may be retained by the Archive, located elsewhere, or temporarily unavailable.

An `Archive.Record` is retained data associated with one Artifact. Records may preserve Archive bureaucracy, identity information, current and historical locations, observations, descriptions, fingerprints, and other hints about that Artifact.

`Tarav.Archive` records Artifacts and Records without regard to their origin, purpose, or meaning. Tarav must use the Archive to record `User.Touched.Data`; the Archive itself does not recognize or distinguish that data from anything else it records.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 73beb42996d3 -->

The Archive does not interpret the internal semantic structure of Artifacts. Consumers construct organization and meaning from Archive Artifacts and Records.

Archive Records do not need to agree. The Archive preserves attributed claims and observations without endorsing their correctness or meaning.

Archive Artifacts are immutable signal. A changed Artifact is another Artifact. Archive Records describing an Artifact are amendable: locations, annotations, fingerprints, and other information may evolve while the Record continues to describe the same Artifact.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 843ff542a6db -->
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 1278026470b5 -->

The Archive provides typed references whose contracts consumers must be able to inspect. A reference to an amendable Record follows its declared contract. The Archive must never silently provide a different Artifact in place of the identified Artifact. If it offers a substitute or another representation, it must make the substitution and its relationship to the requested Artifact explicit.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 461b2a55511f -->
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb cd281677c0ea -->

The Archive must help consumers locate Artifacts. When an Artifact is unavailable, the Archive must expose its retained location history, fingerprints, External Descriptors, and other available hints.

Archive Record coverage may be progressive and demand-driven. Tarav must permit Records to be enriched over time and must not require complete Record coverage as a precondition for capture, reference, or use.

Archive Records must favor representations cheap enough to retain broadly. Records have greater retention priority than the Artifacts they describe. When preservation tradeoffs are unavoidable, the Archive should discard an Artifact before its associated Records, while strongly prioritizing preservation of `User.Touched.Data`.

Consumers may register Artifacts as `External.Descriptors` of other Artifacts. An External Descriptors Record contains attributed references to other Artifacts declared to be useful descriptions, representations, or recovery hints for its target Artifact.

The Archive preserves External Descriptor references without endorsing their correctness or meaning. Each External Descriptor remains an ordinary Artifact with its own identity, locations, Records, and possible External Descriptors.

The Archive does not provide a general semantic relationship graph. Relationships beyond its bounded External Descriptor references, and the assessment of those relationships, belong to consumers such as `Tarav.Diagram`.

`Tarav.Archive` makes no commitment to downstream readers about Record formatting or which context a Record contains. Its responsibility is preservation, not presentation; readers are responsible for interpreting what it preserves.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 779ab9387f69 -->

## Tarav.Diagram

Tarav must provide an extensible Diagram capability for users and agents to express, navigate, and query semantic relationships. The Diagram is a place where users and agents can write ideas, observations, hypotheses, plans, and relationships, including relationships between runtime objects.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 1ab6e69980db -->

Workflows may define specialized semantics and grounding requirements for the material they place there. Relationships about `User.Touched.Data` are one application of this capability. Inclusion in the Diagram does not itself imply truth, validation, or grounding in archived evidence; Archive links and Assertion scores are not universal requirements for Diagram content.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb ad5919d18657 -->

## Contextualization

Tarav must provide extensible tooling and systems for selecting and presenting `Tarav.Diagram` content to collaborative user-agent sessions.

Context may begin with compact Ship editions or Annotations, but Tarav must preserve a navigable path from each contextualized Record to its linked supporting data.

Agents and other consumers must be able to expand that path on demand and inspect progressively deeper supporting context.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb a6d682f872ea -->


## Reference Contracts

Tarav references are typed. Their Types declare the contract under which data is identified and resolved. Some contracts permit maintenance such as schema changes; others commit to exact bytes.

References must never silently deliver data that violates their declared contract. They must provide a way to check for changes relevant to that contract. Hashes and retained hints can support these checks.
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 2c09edaf5ab9 -->
<!-- tarav.breadcrumb 4b3b5219ff55 -->
